findings.where: Article specimen: the pull quote “Whichever PPP Law I am currently working on with a client country!” (desktop and phone)
findings.fault: The pull quote is set in logo blue. The palette gives that blue to the wordmark, links and the button, and the specimen's one real link sits a few lines below in the same blue. A large blue phrase in the middle of the article reads as a link, but it is static (parts.txt p26), so a click does nothing. Because the house reserves the link colour, this is a borrowed property.
findings.who_objects: The bank official reading Mark's article, who clicks the blue quote expecting a source or related paper and gets nothing. Angélique, who will find the blue means link in one place and emphasis in another when she adds posts.

findings.where: Header nav: “Articles” and “Blog” as two separate items (desktop and phone)
findings.fault: The site offers two places for writing with no visible difference between them. The specimen makes it worse: it labels a post “MMM Infra Blog No. 8” on a page called “An article page”, and lists a lecture PDF under it. A visitor can't tell where Mark's PPP law papers live.
findings.who_objects: An official checking whether Mark has written on PPP law frameworks, who has to open both sections to find out and may give up after one.

findings.where: Hero, first screen: the “Get in touch” button and the line under the headline
findings.fault: The only contact route is a mailto button, and Mark's email address is shown nowhere. Next to the action, the proof is a size claim (“Over 40 years of international infrastructure experience”), with no named body, country or PPP law he has worked on. Apart from the one World Bank role, nothing shows that he has done this kind of work for organisations like theirs.
findings.who_objects: A development-bank official on a managed work machine where mailto opens nothing, or who needs to paste the address into a procurement shortlist. The same reader screens advisors against terms of reference by project kind and region, so an adjective claim gives them nothing to check.

findings.where: Motion sketch: the principle words “precise, light, quick” and the single heading-rise it times
findings.fault: The motion character is “quick”, and the one move sketched is a generic heading reveal. The client asked for calm first, with smooth animation built around the aqueduct and the logo built by the opening. The tile sets a motion voice that pulls against that, and shows nothing of how the mark itself would move.
findings.who_objects: Mark, who asked for a calm opening built around the aqueduct and will read “quick” as the opposite. The animation round (#9) would inherit a principle that doesn't fit his brief.

findings.where: Hero at phone width: the portrait stand-in below the button
findings.fault: On phone, Mark's picture falls below the call to action and off the first screen. It is a pale block pushed in from the left with an empty strip beside it, which reads as a misaligned box rather than a figure bleeding off the edge. The visitor asks before they see who is asking.
findings.who_objects: An official opening the site on a phone from a LinkedIn link, who is asked to get in touch before seeing the person. The brief puts the man himself first, and the layout as drawn hides him.

findings.where: Style tile: the section labels “Texture” and “Motion sketch” (with a hairline under them) against “Palette”, “Type pair” and “An article page” (with none); the Source Sans 3 specimen set in the right column without its own label
findings.fault: Section labels of the same rank get two treatments: the right column's labels have a rule under them and the left column's don't. The Source Sans sample floats in the right column, offset from the Gelasio sample, so it reads as a separate section rather than half of the type pair.
findings.who_objects: Mark and the layout-round designer reading the tile as a spec, who can't tell whether the label rule is part of the look or an accident.

findings.where: Motion sketch heading “precise, light, quick” and the type pair note
findings.fault: The tile says Source Sans 3 is for “the nav, buttons, labels and dates only”, then sets the motion sketch's heading in Source Sans. The tile breaks its own type rule.
findings.who_objects: Angélique and the next round's designer, who take the tile as the rule and get two answers on what face a heading takes.

findings.where: Palette: the Mist swatch (“the portrait stand-in only”) and the caption “The logo's own two colours … on white and nothing else”
findings.fault: The caption claims a two-colour, white-only palette above six swatches. Mist's only job ends when the stand-in is replaced, which leaves a colour with no job in the system.
findings.who_objects: Mark, ruling on whether his colours carry over, who reads a claim that the swatches beside it contradict.
